title: [3.x] Replace `PoolVector` with a wrapper for `LocalVector`
body:
Supersedes #59444
Supersedes #108134

This new version of `PoolVector` should be _much safer_, ,and through the elimination of compaction, _much faster_.

## What problem(s) does this PR solve?

Fixes #69804
Fixes #51852 
Fixes #53665
Fixes #37154
Fixes #69412

Related #35539


## Explanation
`PoolVector` has been a longstanding issue in 3.x, and it's long been my intention to try and replace it. There isn't a lot of code in this PR, but it has taken a *lot* of iterating and testing to figure out ways around the hacks upon hacks that make up the old `PoolVector`, and fix them _properly_, and by the end of it, I'm astonished the old version worked *at all*. :grin:

the old `PoolVector`:
* it has many outstanding bugs (including race conditions)
* there is a maximum limit to the number of allocations
* the technique of compacting memory to prevent fragmentation is no longer a good match to modern hardware with virtual address space
* a lock on one thread would prevent COW from operating correctly on another thread (leading to the infamous _"Can't resize PoolVector if locked"_ engine bug)

#### 4.x
In 4.x, one of the first things reduz did was replace all uses of `PoolVector` with `Vector`. This is not an option in 3.x (for backward compatibility), so I have been gradually working a replacement wrapper `PoolVector` which replaces the global memory pool and uses a different backing store.

### Revising `PoolVector` : safety versus backward compatibility
I have come to the conclusion that the old `PoolVector` is completely unsafe. Particularly it is very thread unsafe, but we are just about getting away with it because Godot 3.x is largely single-threaded in design, and by default runs e.g. the renderer as single threaded.

Some of the methods that the old `PoolVector` allows (such as allowing extensive modification to locked `PoolVectors`) probably cannot be fixed to be safe _by design_. So fixing up `PoolVector` is inevitably a compromise between _safety_ and _compatibility_.

Here I've gone for a totally safe design, and ensured the engine runs great (under tested conditions). But it is possible there will be rarely used codepaths that exists that uses the old assumptions, that must be fixed up to use the new safe design.

I have already done this for `Image`, which attempted things like nested `Writes` (and was responsible for many of the existing bugs, see e.g. #69412 ).

It is also very possible to _loosen_ the constraints of this new version, if we get problems due to backward compatibility. I have an alternative branch that performs COW more similarly to the old version. But I would prefer if possible to move to the new safe method, and fix up any existing code that crops up - these often represent live bugs that hadn't been reported yet.

UPDATE: Further testing with user projects has revealed that my tightening up of `Image` locking safety in this PR was too much, where `Image::blit` funcs were users interspersed with locking. So I've relaxed the `Image` locking in #122125 as a follow up. But it's nice to keep them separate commits as they are only indirectly related.

## This version
* analogous to the change in Godot 4.x to use `PackedByteArray` etc, while preserving compatibility for 3.x 
* uses `SafeRefCount` and `thread_local` storage for **local locks**
* like the original, outside of a `read`, elements are returned by value, preventing dangling references when the backing store is resized etc.
* Removes `pool_allocator` completely, as no longer required
* Memory tracking stats are not yet implemented (better for follow up)
* Adds move semantics to `PoolVector` _and_ `Read` and `Write` (this needs checking by reviewer)
* Reused existing `Span` functions wherever possible instead of duplicating functions, to reduce bug surface (which was a problem with the old version)
* Add extensive usage guidelines to the cpp file. The old `PoolVector` (and indeed many of our containers) was sadly lacking in instructions for safe and efficient use.

### Read and Writes claim joint ownership over the `Shared` data
This is a change over the original `PoolVector`, making it far safer to use. If a `read` or `write` still is present after the `PoolVector` is destroyed, the data is not destroyed and only is deleted when the `Access` is destroyed.

### Improved Thread Safety
* `PoolVector` instances using the same backing store can be passed to different threads (i.e. across to servers)
* Provides error messages when the user tries to mutate (e.g. resize etc) while the backing store is locked _on that thread_. But in a bug fix, if the backing store is mutated on a separate thread, the data will successfully COW. We thus have user protection against bugs, and a fix for the client server COW problem.

The old usage of `PoolVector` passing to servers was more single threaded in design, and didn't systematically take advantage of COW to isolate client data from server data.

This PR features a properly thread-orientated implementation, and we change the existing `VisualServer` interface to pass `PoolVector` _by value_ instead of `const ref`. This ensures that if the client attempts to change the data after passing it to the server, the server will be unaffected (both by race conditions, and by unintended changes to the data).

If the client (or server) now modifies a `PoolVector` after the handoff, they will simply COW, and the operation will continue as expected, and the data on each side will be isolated. If they don't modify the data, there will be no COW, and thus no performance cost. We therefore have safety and speed, and it solves the longstanding "Can't resize PoolVector if locked" bug.

## Changes to `LocalVector`
* removed references to `PoolVector` in `LocalVector` (for conversions), and instead expand the support for `Span` so these conversions can take place generically via `Span` (we are trying to move this way in 4.x too)
* consolidated the reallocation code into a single `_realloc` function
* backported the `resize_initialized()` logic from 4.x. This really helped with fulfilling the `PoolVector` requirement that all elements be zeroed / initialized on resize.
* a few misc modernisations from 4.x (e.g. using `copy_arr` to take advantage of `memcpy`).

The change to `Span` for conversions made it easier to have `PoolVector` depend on `LocalVector` without circular includes. There are a couple of minor tweaks at call sites to make it work correctly with `span`.

## GDNative
According to my testing, GDNative seems to be fully compatible with the new `PoolVector` (thanks largely to the size being identical).

<details>

I'm by no means expert with GDNative (never having used it before), but it was something I wanted to verify would work with the new `PoolVector` or whether changes would be needed to the ABI.

* both the old `PoolVector` and the new `PoolVector` both contain exactly 1 pointer, their sizes are identical
* this suggested that binary compatibility might be possible

I believe that although GDNative requires the size to be fixed (for storing internally), the changes to the `PoolVector` are made via a C API to the main engine, therefore it should work seamlessly (I hope) and be binary backwards compatible with existing GDNative libraries.

### GDNative Testing
But I needed to test this, so I have built the GDNative example:
https://docs.godotengine.org/en/3.6/tutorials/scripting/gdnative/gdnative_cpp_example.html

* I have confirmed the example first worked with current 3.x (3.7 dev)
* I built the gdnative example library against 3.x
* I then ran the NEW engine with this PR (new `PoolVector`) and loaded the previously compiled example
* It ran fine

In order to make sure I was testing specifically the `PoolVector` I added the following function to GDNative:

```
PoolIntArray GDExample::get_numbers() {
	PoolIntArray my_array;

	my_array.resize(3);

	PoolIntArray::Write w = my_array.write();
	w[0] = 10;
	w[1] = 20;
	w[2] = 30;

	return my_array;
}
```
I then accessed this from gdscript in the Godot engine:
```
func _ready():
	var pa = $Sprite.get_numbers()
	verify(pa)
	pass


func verify(array) -> void:
	if typeof(array) != TYPE_INT_ARRAY:
		print("Failed: Return value is not a PoolIntArray!")
		return
		
	if array.size() != 3:
		print("Failed: Expected size 3, got ", array.size())
		return
		
	print("Received PoolIntArray: ", array)
	
	if array[0] == 10 and array[1] == 20 and array[2] == 30:
		print("Success.")
	else:
		print("Failed: Elements do not match")
```
Result: Success :partying_face: 

</details>

### GDNative further testing now complete (all with asan)
- [x] multithreaded mutation :heavy_check_mark: 
- [x] cross boundary COW modification :heavy_check_mark: 
- [x] high frequency leak loop :heavy_check_mark: 

## C#
As far as I can make out, c# marshals data to and from `PoolVector`, and stores data using c# types rather than holding references to `PoolVector`, so it should work _as is_ (API compatibility).

## Performance Benchmarking (release)

| version | push_back 1M ints | read / sum 1M ints (locked) | modify 1M ints (locked with `Write`) | continuous resizing |
| ---- | ---- | ---- | ----| ---- |
| old | 61038 us | 280 us | 89 us | 953 us |
| this PR | 4321 us | 192 us | 92 us | 48 us |
| improvement | 14x | 1.45x | 0.97x | 20x |

I'm actually blown away by the performance improvements. I primarily wrote this for the stability improvements over the old `PoolVector`, but the performance blows it away. The only exception is the `Write` locked modifications, where the difference is within the margin of error, they are probably running the same assembly as before.

## Additional information

## Testing
Tested with as many projects as I have as I go along, also using `asan` to identify heap corruption / dangling pointers etc. See also the GDNative testing above as that includes rigorous testing for leaks / multithread access.

As much testing as possible by others would be appreciated, just downloading the artifacts and trying on games would be great.

_Platforms tested:_
- [x] Linux
- [x] Android
- [x] Windows
- [x] Web
- [x] GDNative
- [x] GDScript
- Mac - no test device
- iOS - no test device

## Review & Roadmap
`PoolVector` is one of the major architectural features of 3.x, and although this PR has been tested as thoroughly as possible (both statically and empirically) it will have to be tested in the wild.

This PR is admittedly *huge*, if not in line count, in logical complexity. I always prefer when possible to use small incremental changes, but the nature of this area is that changing `PoolVector` snowballs, it requires fixes to `LocalVector`, `VisualServer` interface, `Image` and a few call sites. It has to be fixed _as one_, else each individual change becomes unstable.

For this reason it makes sense to have a decent period of testing in 3.7 dev versions, while we retain 3.6 as _stable_. The idea of 3.7 is to "go crazy" as much as possible (as it is likely to be the last major 3.x release), even to the extent of fixing longstanding architectural issues. If there are problems it is easy to revert and fix / re-evaluate.

### AI disclosure
_As is policy, I wrote all the code, however I did use Google AI to:_
* help identify several bugs / vulnerabilities in the new versions as I went along (particularly thread safety). (_all fixes were added manually_)
* write a benchmark function in c++ (is not in the PR, that was just to produce the figures in the table)

## Future work
This version uses 2 indirections to access the actual data. `PoolVector` -> `SharedData` -> `LocalVector`.
On the face of it, this isn't super efficient, however if you look at the performance figures, the improvements to locking etc create a much faster system.
On the other hand it may be possible to move over eventually to a system more like `CowData`, where the data is stored with the `SharedData`, and removing one of the indirections. But that's for another day.
